sentences: Lion's Mane & Ashwagandha: Lots of people take these for focus and stress, but I'd leave both out.
People say these herbs left them with anhedonia (when nothing feels good anymore) and sexual dysfunction that persisted even after they stopped, in rare cases reported on forums and YouTube.
Nobody has studied these effects in the two herbs yet, but regulators already warn that SSRIs and finasteride can leave the same kind behind.

fable: All three sentences are built the same way, a claim followed by its qualification, and two of them turn on ", but". Every claim arrives already hedged and sourced ("rare cases", "nobody has studied", "regulators already warn"), which gives it the evenness of a careful summary more than of someone talking.
haiku: The paragraph's rhythm is evenly balanced, with each sentence built to hedge, qualify and pivot in a similar way, which reads smoothly rather than in the uneven rhythm of a single writer's voice.
sonnet: The paragraph is built as a tidy, compact unit (claim, hedged evidence, gap in research, authoritative analogy) with evenly measured sentences and no tangents, which reads as assembled rather than spoken. Its voice stays careful and neutral throughout, with no personal detail, aside or rough edge.
